one_liner: Sogou's C++11 async task engine; its embedded HTTP server hit ~2.2-2.6x nginx's QPS on small bodies (first-party test).
what_it_does: Workflow is a C++11 library for building asynchronous backend services, not a standalone web server. You embed a WFHttpServer in your own program and give it a std::function<void(WFHttpTask*)> that fills in the response. There is no reply() call: the response goes out automatically once every task in that request's SeriesWork has finished. The same task model (series, parallel, DAG, timers, counters, file IO, compute tasks) also drives the built-in async HTTP, Redis, MySQL and Kafka clients and user-defined protocols. It does not replace nginx's configuration: static files, proxying and routing are C++ code you write, and the tutorials include a file server and a proxy.
how_it_is_fast: It is a single-process multi-reactor. N poller threads (mpoller, each fd pinned to poller fd % N) run edge-triggered epoll, or kqueue on BSD/macOS. Each poller reads into its own 256 KB buffer and runs the incremental protocol parser on the poller thread. Complete messages go through a two-list message queue (separate put/get mutexes; the consumer takes the whole list) to a pool of handler threads that run process(). Replies are sent with writev straight from the handler thread and only fall back to EPOLLOUT on EAGAIN. Timeouts sit in a per-poller red-black tree that drives one timerfd, and append_output_body_nocopy() avoids copying the body. In issue #688 the maintainer says the project uses no memory pool and no lock-free structures, and that removing the IO-to-handler queue would add only about 10%.
when_to_use: C++ services that send many small (up to ~4 KB) dynamic HTTP responses over hundreds to ~2K keep-alive connections. This is where the first-party test showed ~2.2-2.6x nginx's QPS and lower latency.

Handlers that fan out to other backends (HTTP, Redis, MySQL, Kafka, custom TCP/TLV protocols) and need async composition that holds no thread while waiting, using series/parallel/DAG tasks instead of callback nesting.
Services that mix network IO with CPU work: compute queues and WFGoTask run in the same task graph as network tasks.

Linux deployments (the primary target; CI builds Ubuntu, Fedora and FreeBSD) where an Apache-2.0 C++11 library with no Boost/asio dependency is wanted. It is packaged as libworkflow-dev (Debian/Ubuntu) and workflow-devel (Fedora).
when_not_to_use: Large responses. In the benchmark, QPS converges with nginx at 16-64 KB bodies (~165K, ~88K, ~45K), and at concurrency 512 with 16/32 KB bodies workflow latency (~8/~18 ms) is about twice nginx's (~4/~9 ms).

Tens of thousands of concurrent connections. No data above 2048 concurrency is published. In issue #906 the maintainer says the published concurrency range (hundreds to a few thousand) was chosen as typical and favorable, and that nginx degraded less above ~10K in their own tests. The default max_connections is 2000.

You need HTTP/2, HTTP/3 or HTTP/1.1 pipelining. The source tree has no HTTP/2 code (issue #129 from 2020 only says it is planned). Server-side pipelining was rejected by design (issue #908): a pipelined connection got one response and was then closed.
You want a configurable nginx replacement for TLS termination, static files or reverse proxying. Workflow is a library, and all of that is C++ you write and maintain.

Handler code that blocks (synchronous DB drivers, sleeps, std::future). By default only 20 handler threads run process() and callbacks, and the FAQ warns that std::future can deadlock all of them. Use counter/timer/go tasks or WFFuture instead.

integration.form: static lib and shared lib (CMake or make; xmake and Bazel files included; distro packages libworkflow-dev / workflow-devel)
integration.dependencies: OpenSSL 1.1+ or BoringSSL (the nossl branch removes it), pthread; zlib, lz4, zstd and snappy only when the Kafka client is built
integration.min_toolchain: C++11 (the library builds with -std=c++11 -fno-exceptions, C sources -std=gnu90), CMake 3.10+; the benchmark used GCC 4.8.5
integration.platforms: Linux (epoll + timerfd), macOS and FreeBSD (kqueue), Android. Windows is a separate IOCP branch. The README claims any CPU (x86 32/64-bit, ARM of either endianness, Loongson).
integration.thread_safety: process() and callbacks run concurrently on handler threads (20 by default). Poller threads (4 by default) do epoll and message parsing. Shared state inside process() needs your own synchronization (the FAQ example guards shutdown() with a flag because process runs concurrently). Handler threads must not block.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: false — a C++ library you link into your own server binary, not a configurable web server or reverse proxy like nginx

gotchas: WFServerParams.max_connections defaults to 2000. Past that, the server closes an idle keep-alive connection or refuses the new one with EMFILE. Raise it for high connection counts (issue #906). The published benchmark code used this default while testing 2048 concurrency.
The response is sent only after all tasks in the server task's series finish, and there is no reply(). Data passed to append_output_body_nocopy() must stay alive until the task callback.

The headline license is Apache-2.0, but src/kernel/rbtree.c is Linux-kernel code under a GPL v2-or-later header, and the repo ships LICENSE_GPLV2. Have the license reviewed before embedding it in proprietary binaries.
The library is compiled with -fno-exceptions, so do not let exceptions escape process() or callbacks. Tasks you create but never start must be released with dismiss().
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick Workflow over H2O when the HTTP server is one piece of a C++ backend that also calls Redis/MySQL/Kafka/HTTP upstreams asynchronously. H2O's catalogued win over nginx is static-file serving, while Workflow's is small dynamic responses. Drogon, Crow and Oat++ are catalogued only against Go net/http on the-benchmarker, so Workflow is the only one in this group with a head-to-head against nginx, although that comparison is first-party.
verified_claims_summary: The authors' 2020 test ran wrk from a second identical machine: Xeon E5-2630 v4 (40 cores), 192 GB RAM, 25 GbE, CentOS 7.8 with kernel 3.10, GCC 4.8.5; optimization flags were not stated, and the library's CMake default is RelWithDebInfo. It served a fixed random body with Date/Content-Type headers, with workflow on 16 pollers + 20 handlers and nginx on 40 workers. Read off the charts, at concurrency 256-2048 workflow reached ~490-530K QPS vs nginx's ~203-213K for 64 B/512 B bodies and ~426-458K vs ~180-205K for 4 KB (~2.2-2.6x), but the curves converge at 16-64 KB and nginx had lower latency at concurrency 512 with 16/32 KB bodies.
status_note: Actively maintained: v1.1.0 was released 2026-08-10 after a run of fix releases (TLS concurrency, HTTP parser byte-by-byte bug, >2 GB size handling), with 14.4k stars and Debian/Fedora packages. The README says it serves Sogou's back-end services at more than 10 billion requests per day. It is Apache-2.0, apart from the GPL-headed rbtree.c.
